(CNN) -- Voters in Nashville, Tennessee -- a city that has seen a dramatic increase in its immigrant population -- rejected a measure Thursday that would have made English the only language used for government business in its metropolitan area. Nearly 57 percent of those who cast ballots Thursday in Nashville, Tennessee, voted against the measure. With all 173 precincts reporting, 41,752 voters, or nearly 57 percent, voted against the proposed amendment, with 32,144 voters supporting it, according to unofficial results posted on the Nashville city government Web site. "No person shall have a right to government services in any other language," the proposal read. The measure would have included government meetings. The Metropolitan Council, which submitted the measure, could have mandated exceptions to protect public health and safety. Elise Shore, southeast director of the Mexican-American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, said her regional office in Atlanta, Georgia, was monitoring the Nashville balloting. "We just elected our first black president. There are the forces of globalization and conducting business around the world ... in the face of this, we see these measures?" Shore asked. The proposal "sends a strong message ... this is a negative message. In fact, it invites discrimination," she said. In a newspaper editorial published Thursday, The Tennessean urged voters to defeat the proposal. "This amendment would exclude and marginalize those residents and visitors to Nashville simply because English is not their native tongue," the editorial said. The polls opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 7 p.m. Before the measure was defeated, a spokesman for U.S. English Inc., an action group that supports English-only laws nationwide, said the Nashville proposal was a good one. "Government programs are aimed at helping people reach self-sufficiency and success," Rob Toonkel said. "Allowing use of a second language doesn't encourage them to learn English." "The key word [of the amendment] is 'actions that bind the government,' " Toonkel said, which would cover transactions such as getting a city contract. If a non-English speaker needs help filling out a form, and someone in that agency speaks their language, they should be helped, he said. "But you shouldn't be able to come in, pick up a form [in another language] and leave." According to Toonkel, about 30 states and more than 100 localities have made English their official language, and he said his organization believes such laws are legal. Raul Gonzalez, legislative director for the National Council of La Raza, said the message of the proposal is discriminatory. "What it ... says is, 'If you speak a language other than English, you may not be welcome here,' " Gonzalez said. La Raza is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization focused on reducing poverty and discrimination and improving opportunities for Hispanic Americans. Gonzalez said similar English-only laws across the country "have so many exceptions they are meaningless." In an editorial earlier this month, The Tennessean quoted the referendum's sponsor, Councilman Eric Crafton, who said the bill was needed to save the city $100,000 to $150,000 in annual translation and related costs. However, metro officials told the newspaper such services are provided by employees already on the city's payroll. The council passed a similar bill in 2007, but it was vetoed by then-Mayor Bill Purcell, who called it "unconstitutional, unnecessary and mean-spirited," according to The Tennessean. U.S. Census data from 2000 showed an increase of 210 percent in the immigrant population of the Nashville metro area, including Davidson County, since 1990. During that decade, immigrants accounted for 45 percent of the overall population increase in the city. More than two-thirds, or 67 percent, of the area's foreign-born population had entered since 1990. This was much higher than the rate for the state overall, which was about 58 percent. The Census Bureau's American Community Survey, taken between 2005 and 2007 for the Nashville metro area, shows a population of 613,632. Of that number, 61,843 were foreign-born, with most of the immigrants coming from Latin America. About 73,000 residents speak a language other than English at home and, of those, 35,290 speak English less than "very well," the survey found.

# The 2009 "English First" Referendum in Nashville, Tennessee

## The Outcome

On January 22, 2009, voters in Nashville (Davidson County) **rejected** a ballot measure that would have made English the official language of the metropolitan government. The proposal failed by a margin of approximately **57% to 43%**, with turnout notably high for a special election.

The measure, sometimes referred to as the "English First" or "English Only" amendment, would have required most government communications and official actions to be conducted in English, with limited exceptions (such as those required by federal law or necessary for public health and safety).

## Background

The referendum was championed by Councilman Eric Crafton, who had pushed the initiative through a petition drive after earlier legislative efforts stalled. Nashville was one of the largest American cities to vote on such a measure, drawing national attention as a test case for language policy in a city experiencing significant immigrant population growth.

## Supporters' Arguments

Proponents of the measure generally argued that:

- **Unity and assimilation:** A common language would promote social cohesion and encourage immigrants to integrate into American society.
- **Cost savings:** Limiting government translation and multilingual document services would reduce taxpayer expenses.
- **Practical governance:** Conducting official business in a single language would streamline government operations.
- **Incentive to learn English:** Supporters contended that the policy would encourage non-English speakers to acquire language skills valuable for economic advancement.

## Opponents' Arguments

Those against the measure countered that:

- **Economic harm:** Business leaders, including the Nashville Area Chamber of Commerce, warned the measure would damage the city's image and hurt its ability to attract businesses, conventions, and international investment.
- **Discrimination and tone:** Critics argued the measure was divisive, unwelcoming, and sent a message of intolerance toward immigrants and visitors.
- **Public safety concerns:** Opponents noted potential complications in communicating essential health and safety information to non-English speakers.
- **Unnecessary:** Many felt existing conditions did not warrant the law and that it addressed a problem that did not meaningfully exist.
- **Broad coalition of opposition:** Then-Mayor Karl Dean, business organizations, religious groups, and civic leaders publicly campaigned against it.

## Significance

The vote was widely interpreted as a signal that a diverse, growing Southern city prioritized an inclusive and business-friendly reputation over restrictive language legislation. The outcome was cited in subsequent national debates as an example of a major city rejecting official-English policies, and it reflected the influence of business and civic coalitions in shaping the result.

# City Ballot Measure to Make English Sole Language of Government Fails at Polls

*Contentious proposal draws sharp divide between officials and immigrant advocacy groups*

---

**CITY DESK** — Voters rejected a controversial ballot measure Tuesday that would have established English as the only language permitted for official city government business, ending a months-long campaign that exposed deep divisions over immigration, civic access, and the region's rapidly diversifying population.

Measure 14, which failed by a margin of 58 to 42 percent according to unofficial results released early Wednesday, would have required all municipal documents, public meetings, government websites, and official communications to be conducted exclusively in English. The measure carved out limited exceptions for emergency services, public health notices, and functions mandated by federal or state law.

## What the Measure Would Have Done

Had it passed, Measure 14 would have eliminated the city's current practice of providing translated materials—including ballots, tax documents, and permit applications—in six languages. It also would have discontinued interpreter services at public council meetings and required the removal of multilingual signage at city facilities within one year.

Supporters estimated the measure would save the city roughly $2.3 million annually in translation and interpretation costs, though opponents disputed that figure, arguing it failed to account for legal challenges and reduced government efficiency.

## Supporters Cite Unity and Cost

Councilmember Raymond Doyle, who sponsored the measure, expressed disappointment with the outcome but defended the proposal's intent.

"This was never about excluding anyone," Doyle said in a statement Wednesday. "It was about promoting a common language that unites us as a community and ensuring taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly. English is the language of opportunity in this country, and encouraging its use serves newcomers as much as anyone."

The measure drew support from a coalition of taxpayer advocacy organizations and residents who argued that a single official language would streamline government operations.

"We're a nation of immigrants, and every generation before learned English," said Margaret Ellison, spokesperson for Citizens for Government Efficiency, which backed the measure. "We simply asked that the government conduct its official business in one language. The voters disagreed, and we respect that, but this conversation isn't over."

## Officials Warn of Legal and Practical Problems

City Attorney Denise Alvarado had previously cautioned that the measure could expose the city to litigation under federal civil rights law, particularly Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on national origin in programs receiving federal funding.

"Provisions requiring meaningful access for limited-English-proficient residents are well established in federal law," Alvarado said. "A blanket English-only policy would have almost certainly triggered legal challenges the city would have struggled to defend."

Mayor Patricia Nguyen, who publicly opposed the measure, praised the outcome as a reflection of the city's values.

"Our residents made clear that access to government is a right, not a privilege reserved for those who already speak English fluently," Nguyen said at a press conference. "When a senior citizen can't understand her property tax bill, or a parent can't read a notice about school enrollment, that's not efficiency—that's a barrier. I'm proud of what our community said today."

## Immigrant Rights Groups Celebrate

For immigrant advocacy organizations, which mobilized heavily against the measure, the defeat marked a significant victory following an intense grassroots campaign.

"This is a tremendous relief for the tens of thousands of families who rely on translated materials just to participate in civic life," said Luis Herrera, executive director of the Coalition for Immigrant Justice. "Language access isn't a luxury. It's how people pay their taxes, access health care, and show up for their kids at school. Today, our neighbors were told they belong here."

Herrera's organization estimated that nearly one in four city residents speaks a language other than English at home, with significant Spanish, Vietnamese, Mandarin, and Tagalog-speaking communities.

Anh Tran, a volunteer with a local refugee resettlement nonprofit, described going door-to-door in immigrant neighborhoods for weeks leading up to the vote.

"I met a woman who has lived here for fifteen years, works two jobs, and is still learning English," Tran said. "She was terrified she wouldn't be able to renew her business license or understand a jury summons. People like her are the heart of this city. This vote protects them."

## A Divided Electorate

Political analysts said the measure reflected broader national tensions over immigration and cultural identity that have surfaced in municipalities across the country.

"Language policy has become a proxy for larger debates about who belongs and what it means to be part of a community," said Dr. Harold Kim, a political science professor at the state university. "The fact that this measure got 42 percent of the vote tells you the underlying anxieties are real, even if voters ultimately rejected this particular approach."

Precinct-level results showed the measure performing strongly in older, less diverse neighborhoods while failing decisively in areas with larger immigrant populations and among younger voters.

## What Comes Next

Doyle indicated he may pursue a narrower version of the policy focused solely on cost transparency, while opponents pledged to remain vigilant.

"We'll be watching," Herrera said. "The result today was clear, but we know these efforts have a way of returning. Our communities will keep organizing to make sure everyone has a seat at the table."

For now, the city's existing language-access policies remain in place, and translated materials will continue to be available across municipal services.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as final results are certified.*

---

*Reporting by the City Desk. Additional contributions from staff writers.*

# Nashville Voters Reject English-Only Measure in Decisive Vote

*A ballot initiative that would have made English the sole language of government operations fails at the polls*

NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Voters in Nashville and Davidson County soundly rejected a controversial ballot measure Thursday that would have required most government business to be conducted exclusively in English, delivering a defeat to the initiative's chief architect, Metro Councilman Eric Crafton.

## The Vote

The measure, known as "English First," failed by a margin of approximately 57 to 43 percent, with roughly 41,000 voters opposing the amendment and 32,000 supporting it. The special election drew significant attention both locally and nationally, positioning Nashville as a test case for how growing Southern cities would navigate questions of immigration and cultural integration.

Had it passed, the amendment would have made Nashville the largest U.S. city to adopt such a sweeping English-only requirement, mandating that official government communications, documents, and meetings be conducted in English, with limited exceptions for matters involving health and safety.

## A Divisive Campaign

Crafton, a Republican councilman, had pushed the measure for several years, arguing it would promote unity, encourage immigrants to learn English, and save taxpayer money on translation services. The special election itself, held in January, was estimated to cost taxpayers several hundred thousand dollars.

Opposition to the measure formed a broad coalition that included Mayor Karl Dean, business leaders, religious organizations, and immigrant advocacy groups. Critics argued the amendment would harm the city's economic competitiveness, damage its national reputation, and marginalize a growing immigrant community that had contributed to the region's revitalization.

Business leaders, in particular, warned that the measure could deter corporations and international investment, complicating efforts to attract companies and conventions to the area.

## A Changing City

The debate unfolded against the backdrop of Nashville's rapidly diversifying population. According to U.S. Census figures, the foreign-born population of the Nashville metropolitan area grew dramatically in the preceding decades, transforming what had long been a relatively homogeneous Southern city.

Census data indicated that immigrants comprised roughly 10 percent of Davidson County's population, with the region experiencing one of the fastest-growing immigrant populations in the nation. The city became home to substantial communities of Hispanic, Kurdish, Somali, Vietnamese, and Laotian residents, among others. Nashville notably hosted one of the largest Kurdish populations in the United States, earning parts of the city the informal nickname "Little Kurdistan."

The number of residents speaking a language other than English at home had climbed into the tens of thousands, reflecting decades of migration drawn by the area's economic opportunities and relatively affordable cost of living.

## Reactions

Opponents celebrated the outcome as an affirmation of Nashville's welcoming character.

"The people of Nashville have said that we are a welcoming and friendly city, and that we're going to reach out to everyone," Mayor Dean said following the results, framing the vote as a decision about the city's identity and future.

Crafton, for his part, expressed disappointment but defended his intentions, maintaining that the measure was never intended to divide the community but to strengthen it through a common language.

## Broader Significance

The Nashville vote was closely watched by observers across the country as immigration debates intensified nationally. For a city working to establish itself as a modern, economically dynamic hub of the New South, the outcome was widely interpreted as a statement about the direction Nashville intended to take.

The defeat of the English-only amendment suggested that even in a traditionally conservative region, appeals to inclusivity and economic pragmatism could prevail over efforts to restrict the role of languages other than English in public life.

---

*Note: This piece reflects the general contours of the January 2009 Nashville referendum. For publication, specific vote totals, census figures, and direct quotations should be verified against official election records and primary sources.*

# Southern City Rejects English-Only Ordinance After Contentious Debate

*Council votes 4-3 against measure that would have required official government business be conducted in English*

---

**RIVERSIDE, [State]** — After months of heated public debate and a packed council chamber that drew residents on both sides of the issue, the Riverside City Council voted 4-3 Tuesday night to reject a proposed ordinance that would have established English as the city's sole official language for government operations.

The measure would have required all official city documents, meetings, and public communications to be conducted exclusively in English, with limited exceptions for emergency services and federally mandated services.

The vote followed nearly four hours of public comment, during which more than 60 residents addressed the council.

## Supporters Express Disappointment

Advocates for the ordinance argued the measure would have promoted unity and encouraged immigrant integration while reducing municipal costs associated with translation services.

A representative from U.S. English Inc., a national organization that advocates for official English legislation, expressed disappointment with the outcome.

"We're disappointed that the council chose to reject a common-sense measure that has been adopted by more than 30 states and hundreds of municipalities," said a spokesperson for the organization. "Establishing English as the official language of government isn't about excluding anyone—it's about encouraging immigrants to learn the common language that unites us as Americans and empowers them to fully participate in civic life. A shared language strengthens communities."

The organization noted that similar ordinances have been upheld in various jurisdictions and framed the effort as protecting taxpayer resources.

## Opponents Celebrate the Decision

Civil rights organizations and immigrant advocacy groups, which had mobilized heavily against the ordinance, welcomed the council's decision.

A representative from UnidosUS (formerly the National Council of La Raza) characterized the vote as a victory for inclusion.

"Tonight, the Riverside City Council chose community over division," the spokesperson said. "English-only laws don't help anyone learn English—there are already waiting lists for English classes across this country. What these measures actually do is send a message that some residents aren't welcome and create real barriers for families trying to access basic city services, from paying a water bill to reporting a crime. We commend the council for recognizing that."

The Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF), which had submitted a letter to council members warning of potential legal concerns, also praised the outcome while cautioning against future efforts.

"English-only ordinances raise serious constitutional and civil rights questions, particularly when they restrict access to government services for limited-English-proficient residents," a MALDEF attorney stated. "Such measures can run afoul of federal protections, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. We're pleased the council declined to expose the city to unnecessary legal risk and, more importantly, chose to keep local government accessible to all of its residents."

## A Divided Community

The ordinance had been introduced three months ago by Councilmember [Name], who argued that the city's growing population made a unified language policy increasingly important for efficient governance.

"This was never about hostility toward any group," the councilmember said following the vote. "It was about establishing clarity and ensuring our limited resources serve everyone effectively. I respect the council's decision, but I believe this conversation isn't over."

Riverside, like many communities across the South, has experienced significant demographic change in recent decades, with its foreign-born population growing substantially. According to census data, roughly [percentage] of city residents speak a language other than English at home.

During public comment, residents offered starkly different perspectives.

"My grandparents came here and learned English, and they expected everyone else to as well," said longtime resident Margaret Coleman, who supported the measure. "There's nothing wrong with asking people to embrace the language of the country they've chosen to call home."

Others described practical hardships.

"My mother has lived here for 20 years and pays her taxes just like everyone else," said resident Carlos Mendoza. "She's still learning English, but she shouldn't have to be turned away when she needs help from her own city government."

## What Comes Next

The council's rejection effectively ends the current proposal, though supporters indicated they may pursue a revised version or a ballot initiative in the future.

Mayor [Name], who did not have a vote on the measure but had voiced reservations, urged residents to move forward together.

"Riverside is stronger when every resident feels they belong here," the mayor said. "I hope tonight marks the beginning of a more constructive conversation about how we serve all our neighbors."

The three council members who supported the ordinance have not indicated whether they will reintroduce the measure.

The organizations mentioned—U.S. English Inc., UnidosUS, and MALDEF—are real entities, and the positions attributed to them reflect their general publicly stated stances on official-English legislation, but the specific quotes are fabricated for this example.*
